_comment: News posts for /news. Newest first. body is a list of paragraphs; a paragraph starting with '## ' is a heading. Link games with {{slug}}.

posts.title: Which Sketchpad Arcade game should you play next?
posts.summary: A practical guide to picking a pencil-drawn puzzle, word challenge, arcade run or two-player game that matches your mood.
body: Sketchpad Arcade looks like a familiar notebook, but the pages do very different things. Some games ask you to make careful pencil marks. Others turn a quick flick or swipe into a high-score challenge. And the Versus games bring back the little games people play with a friend on paper. If you have five minutes—or a whole evening—here is how to pick a game that fits.
## If you want to think without rushing

Start with {{doodle-doku}}, a 9×9 Sudoku grid with three difficulty levels. The goal is to give every row, column and 3×3 box the digits 1 through 9 without repeats. Its Notes control is useful when you want to record possible answers rather than guess. For a different kind of deduction, {{blot-sweeper}} turns minesweeper logic into an ink-blot hunt. A number shows how many blots touch a square, including diagonally; use that information to identify safe squares before opening them.

If sorting is more your style, try {{ink-jars}}. You can pour ink onto a matching color or into an empty jar, and you win by filling jars with one color each. It's more about preserving room for the next pour than tapping quickly. {{paper-gates}} gives you a different spatial puzzle: slide blocks around one another until each reaches a gate of the right color and size.
## If you want a quick challenge with movement

{{doodle-darts}} is a good short choice when you want to test your timing. For something you can improve shot by shot, try {{pencil-putt}}: pull back to set the strength of your putt, then use the ruler walls and desk objects to your advantage. A soft, well-placed shot is often better than full power.

Want more motion? {{sketch-sprint}} is a runner with sharp left and right turns, jumps, slides and eight unlockable characters. {{paper-plane-dash}} moves around the inside of a tube made from construction paper, and collecting stars unlocks more plane designs. Both reward looking ahead rather than reacting at the last possible moment.
## If you enjoy patterns in words

{{sketch-search}} is the relaxed choice: find themed hidden words among letters printed on graph paper. {{word-workshop}} asks you to connect letters in a wheel to fill a crossword; other valid words can earn bonuses. For more reasoning, {{four-in-a-frame}} has sixteen words hiding four groups of four. Try identifying the most obvious group first, then use what's left to uncover the trickier relationships.

{{letter-links}} is the one to try if you like word chains. Every new word begins with the last letter of the previous word, and each letter you use around the path turns gold. Pay attention to your ending letter: finishing a word with a common letter often gives you more options for the next one.
## If you would rather play with a friend

The Versus section gathers games that can be shared rather than just scored alone. In {{box-doodles}}, you draw the fourth side of a box to claim it and take another turn. In {{pencil-pool}}, pull a No. 2 pencil back like a cue, aim at the balls and try to clear your color. {{doodle-kick}} is flick soccer: drag a player back and let go to send it skidding toward the ball. {{guess-my-doodle}} is a draw-and-guess game where one person makes a picture and the other tries to recognize it.

Check each game page for its available play modes. Some can be played on the same device, some against a computer and some by sharing a link with a friend. You never need to guess what the controls are; the How to Play section spells them out.
## What makes this arcade different?

Sketchpad Arcade leans into the paper-and-pencil feeling. The covers use warm sketchbook pages, rough graphite linework, handwritten titles and lightly layered colored-pencil marks. That visual language gives the games a connected feel even when a puzzle and an arcade run play very differently. The sister site, Beach Day Arcade, presents many related ideas in colorful seaside scenes instead.

Still unsure? Try one game from each category—Puzzle, Arcade, Word and Versus—and see which one makes you want another round. Every title on Sketchpad Arcade opens a game page with instructions, tips and a Play button.

posts.title: Five pencil-and-paper strategies for tricky Sketchpad puzzles
posts.summary: Useful moves for Doodle Doku, Blot Sweeper, Crayon Code, Ink Jars and Paper Gates when a puzzle seems stuck.
body: Sometimes the next move isn't difficult because the game is fast; it is difficult because several choices look equally good. The best fix is often to change the question you're asking about the board. Here are five approaches that work in actual Sketchpad Arcade games, with examples you can try immediately.
## 1. Use notes before you commit in Doodle Doku

{{doodle-doku}} follows the standard Sudoku rule: every row, column and 3×3 box needs the digits 1 through 9 exactly once. If you are looking at an empty square and two numbers seem possible, don't guess yet. Turn on Notes and pencil in the candidates. Now look across the same row and down its column. When another number is placed elsewhere, it may eliminate one candidate. An easier first win is to find a nearly complete row or box where only one number is missing.
## 2. Read the neighbors in Blot Sweeper

{{blot-sweeper}} uses ink blots hidden beneath squares. A revealed number tells you how many blots touch that square, including diagonally. If a 1 touches only one still-covered square, that square must be a blot; flag it. If a revealed 2 already has two confirmed blots beside it, the other covered neighbors are safe. Try reading a group of adjacent numbered squares together instead of treating each number as a separate clue. The first opening is safe, so use the information it reveals before racing to tap elsewhere.
## 3. Change only one thing in Crayon Code

In {{crayon-code}}, a hidden arrangement of crayons is waiting to be guessed. Feedback dots tell you how many colors are correct and in the correct position, or correct but in a different position. Once a guess gives you useful feedback, do not rearrange every crayon. Keep one known part of your guess fixed and move the others. That way a change in feedback is easier to interpret. On the harder level, colors can repeat, so avoid assuming each crayon appears only once.
## 4. Keep an empty space for Ink Jars

{{ink-jars}} lets you pour the top color of one jar onto a matching color or into an empty jar. A jar filled with a single color gets corked and is finished. The easy mistake is to use every empty jar too early. Instead, find two jars with matching top colors and combine them where possible. Keeping one jar open as temporary storage gives you more options when a buried color needs to come to the top. Look at what is under the layer you are pouring, not just the color you are moving.
## 5. Clear the right block first in Paper Gates

In {{paper-gates}}, blocks slide through gaps and leave by gates matching their color. The board is crowded, and blocks can't pass through one another. Look for a block that already has a path to a matching gate: removing it can create the space that makes two more moves possible. Check gate width as well as color. A narrow gate won't take a wider block, even when the pencil colors match. Work backwards from the gates and ask which piece must leave first.
## A useful habit across all five

Before each move, ask: What will this open up? A Sudoku note removes uncertainty; a Blot Sweeper flag makes nearby squares safer to judge; a Crayon Code test rules out possibilities; an Ink Jars pour creates space; a Paper Gates move clears an exit. Those are different games, but the same habit works in all of them: use the current move to improve the next decision.

If you prefer something less demanding, start with {{sketch-search}} or a short round of {{pencil-putt}}. For another set of recommendations arranged by mood, read our guide to choosing a Sketchpad game.

posts.title: Seven games for two: the Versus tab
posts.summary: Tic-tac-toe, SOS, dots and boxes, paper boats, four in a row, checkers and draw-and-guess, all for two players. Pass one phone, play the bot, or invite a friend by text.
body: Sketchpad Arcade has had a Versus tab for about a day, and it already holds seven games. They are the games everyone has played on the back page of a notebook when the lecture ran long, and they are the first games on the site built from scratch rather than traced from a Beach Day Arcade twin.
## The notebook classics

{{tic-tac-doodle}} is tic-tac-toe, blue X against pink O. {{doodle-sos}} is SOS on a 6×6 grid: finish S-O-S in a line and you score and go again, and one letter can finish two lines at once. {{box-doodles}} is dots and boxes, 25 boxes so there are no ties, and the part where the long chains start changing hands is as tense as ever. {{paper-boats}} is the hide-and-seek grid game with four folded paper boats on an 8×8 page, where a miss is a splash and a hit is a pencil X.
## Three more this week

{{connect-sketch}} drops coloured-pencil counters down a hand-drawn frame until somebody lines up four. {{sketchers}} is checkers, with crowned pieces and a Hard bot that looks several moves ahead. {{guess-my-doodle}} is the odd one out: you draw a word on the page, your friend watches it appear line by line and guesses, then draws one for you. It is a team game, so the score belongs to both of you.
## Three ways to play

Every Versus game has Play vs Friend, which means passing one phone back and forth. Paper Boats even asks you to hand it over between turns so nobody peeks at the other page. Every game except Guess My Doodle also has a bot on Easy, Medium and Hard, and the game remembers your record against it on your device. Easy is for little ones having their first go against a computer. Hard is a real opponent: the Tic-Tac-Doodle bot never loses, so a draw counts as a win, and the Box Doodles bot gives away as little as it can.

The third way is new. Tap Invite a friend and the game makes a six-letter code and a link you can text to someone. They open it and play pink, you play blue, and you take turns whenever you like, an hour or a day apart. There are no accounts, no names and no chat, and only the person you sent the link to can see the game. Your open games sit in Your Games with Friends on the home page so you can see whose turn it is. It works in six of the seven games; Paper Boats sits it out for now, because we have not yet found a way to keep each player's boats hidden from the other phone.
## And one for the Word tab

{{sketch-with-friends}} arrived in the same batch. It is a crossword tile game on a sketchbook page, with seven paper letter tiles each, double and triple squares, a bot on three levels and Invite a friend. It lives under Word rather than Versus, but it is very much a game for two, and its word list is checked so nothing rude ever lands on the board.

posts.title: Pencil Patrol: Stubby versus the erasers
posts.summary: A maze chase on a notebook page, with four erasers that each move their own way. Notes on drawing it and tuning the erasers.
body: {{pencil-patrol}} is a maze-chase game in the spirit of the arcade classics, and it is the newest game on the site. Stubby, a stubby little pencil, scuttles through coloured-pencil mazes collecting dots while four googly-eyed erasers try to rub him out.
## Four erasers, four habits

The thing that makes a maze chase fun is not the maze, it is the chasers. Each eraser has its own way of moving: Pinky chases you directly, Smudge tries to get ahead of you, Zigzag zigzags, and Dozer gets shy and backs off when you are close. Once you learn those four habits you can play the erasers against each other, which is where the game gets good.
## The gold star

Grab a gold star sticker and the erasers go pale and wobbly for a few seconds. Bonk them back into the pencil case and the points climb: 200, 400, 800, 1600. Saving the star until the erasers are bunched up is the single best trick in the game.

Stubby, the erasers and the mazes are all hand-drawn in pencil for this game, with dark outlines and coloured-pencil cross-hatching inside, which is the look we are moving every Sketchpad game toward. The erasers go back to their corners every so often, which gives you a breather to grab dots. Clear the page and the next one is a little faster.

posts.title: Paper Plane Dash and ten real folds
posts.summary: Our first original Sketchpad game, not a twin of anything. A tube-flying dash on black construction paper, with paper planes you could actually fold.
body: Every game on Sketchpad Arcade so far has been a pencil-sketch twin of a Beach Day Arcade game. {{paper-plane-dash}} is the first one that is ours alone.
## Flying round a tube

The idea started as a lane runner, three lanes wide and three high, with the plane banking as it moved. We built that, played it, and it felt like a lot of other runners. So we tried something else: a round tube, drawn on black construction paper, with the plane flying along the inside wall. You touch the side of the tube you want to be on and the plane rolls round to it the short way, up the sides, over the top and back down, belly to the wall the whole way. It feels like nothing else on either site.
## Real folds

The planes you unlock are all real folds. The Basic Glider, the Bulldog Dart, the Nakamura Lock, the Harrier, the Hammerhead, the Flying Wing, the Canard, the Stunt Plane and the Delta Wing. If you have ever folded one at a desk when you should have been doing something else, it is in the game. Stars unlock them, and every 600 metres turns to a new, faster sector page.

The junk in the tube is drawn from the same desk: crumpled paper balls in every construction-paper colour, erasers, pencil stubs, rulers and ink blots. Fly through a paper ring's gap for 50 points, and every ten stars starts Dart Mode, when your plane fires paper darts that pop everything straight ahead.

posts.title: Why every game got a new name
posts.summary: Sea Merge became Margin Merge, Tide Clash became Draw Brawl. The thinking behind renaming every game on the site, and what is still on the list.
body: When Sketchpad Arcade opened, the games had the same names as their Beach Day Arcade twins. That was fine for a week, and then it was confusing: two sites, the same name, different art. So we renamed all of them.
## From the beach to the desk

The new names come from the sketchbook: {{margin-merge}}, {{doodle-darts}}, {{pencil-putt}}, {{scribble-blocks}}, {{paper-gates}}. A few got a bigger change than a name. Sonar Sub became {{space-blaster}}, a retro shooter on grid paper with UFOs instead of sea creatures. Sea Glass became {{space-glass}}, a colour-by-number of rockets and planets. Gem Cove became {{chibi-chib}}, with big-eyed chibi animals to sort. Beach Link became {{no-2-pencil}}, drawn in plain pencil with classroom doodles that colour in when you tap them.
## Still on the list

Some games have their new name but still carry their beach art inside, and we are working through them one at a time, drawing new characters and scenery to match the sketchbook. The goal for the whole site is the same: dark pencil outlines, bright coloured-pencil cross-hatching, and no ocean in sight. If a game looks a little beachy for now, that is why.
Old links still work. Every old game address redirects to the new one, so anything you bookmarked or shared will still land in the right place.

posts.title: Sketch Sprint, the game that started the site
posts.summary: It began as a request to redraw a boardwalk runner like a sketchbook doodle. It ended up as a whole second site.
body: Sketchpad Arcade exists because of one request: take our sister site's boardwalk runner and make it look like someone drew it in pencil in the back of a sketchbook. We did, and the result was {{sketch-sprint}}.
## What a sketch twin is

A sketch twin is the same game underneath, with every piece of art redrawn in pencil. Same corners, same power-ups, same unlockable runners, but the path twists through downtown, the backyard, the park, a creek and the woods instead of the beach, and the eight runners are hand-drawn characters with backpacks instead of beach animals. Fixes on one side reach the other, which keeps both games honest.
## Why a second site

We thought about offering the sketch look as a toggle inside each game and decided against it. The sketch versions have their own names and their own mood, and they deserve a home where everything matches, right down to the hand-drawn buttons and the graph-paper background. Keeping the sites separate also keeps each one simple: Beach Day Arcade stays bright and painted, and Sketchpad Arcade stays pencil and paper.
Sketch Sprint is still the game we show people first. Swipe the way the arrow points to take each corner, jump the logs, slide under the nets, and collect stars to unlock the rest of the runners.

posts.title: How we decide what makes a Sketchpad Arcade game
posts.summary: The short list of rules every game on the site has to follow before it goes live.
body: Sketchpad Arcade is a two-person-sized studio, and the first question about any game is whether we would actually keep playing it after the first five minutes. That turns into a short list of rules, and every game on the site has to pass all of them.
## The rules
Clean, always. No gore, no gambling mechanics and nothing you would not want on your screen in a library or a lecture hall.
No gambling mechanics. No loot boxes, no spinning wheels, no fake currencies you buy with real money. Progress is earned by playing.
Nothing to install and nobody to sign up. Every game runs in the browser, and your scores and progress are saved on your own device, not on our servers.

Original work. We happily borrow mechanics, because a bubble shooter is a bubble shooter, but every character, drawing and word list on the site is ours. We never use another game's name, art or text.
Drawn by hand. The whole site is meant to look like a page from a sketchbook, so every game's art is pencil on paper, with dark outlines and coloured-pencil inside.
## How a game gets here

New games start on a private preview where we play them ourselves for a few days. Most get changes, some get sent back, and the ones that stick around get their own pencil cover before they go live. The games you see in the New This Week row are the survivors.
If you think something on the site breaks one of these rules, tell us from the contact page. We would rather hear about it than not.

posts.title: Welcome to Sketchpad Arcade
posts.summary: Free browser games drawn like a page from a sketchbook, from a small studio in Pensacola, Florida. What the site is and why we made it.
body: Sketchpad Arcade is a collection of free games you can play in your browser on a phone, tablet or computer, and every one of them is drawn in pencil, like a doodle in the back of a notebook. There is nothing to download and no account to make. It is made by Restless Faith Media, a small independent studio in Pensacola, Florida.
## Why we built it

We already ran Beach Day Arcade, a site of bright, painted beach games. Then we tried redrawing one of them in pencil, as if someone had copied it into a sketchbook, and we liked it so much we wanted a whole site that looked that way. Sketchpad Arcade is that site: the same kind of quick, clean games, on graph paper and lined notebook pages, with dark pencil outlines and coloured-pencil inside.
## What is here

The site opened with sketch twins of the Beach Day games, like {{sketch-sprint}}, {{doodle-drop}}, {{draw-brawl}} and {{margin-merge}}, and has started adding games of its own, beginning with {{paper-plane-dash}}. Every game has its own page with a short guide on how to play, the controls, a few tips and a bit about how it was made.
## What to expect

Clean, always. Hand-drawn art and characters. Progress saved on your device, not ours. And a site that keeps getting a little better every week. If you have an idea for a game, or you found a bug, the contact page is the place to tell us.
